literal: The next younger brother Qu was fierce and changeable, not like Gu's mildness, compliance, and yielding; thereupon the elders Liang Gai and others killed Qu and together urged Gu.
idiomatic: The next brother Qu was brutal and unpredictable, nothing like Gu's mildness; the elders Liang Gai and others killed Qu and pressed Gu to rule.

literal: Gu said, "My elder brother by age should succeed; how could I overstep and occupy the great enterprise?
idiomatic: Gu said, "My elder brother should reign by right. How could I leap over him to seize the throne?

literal: He then went in person to Ye to welcome him, asking to remain himself as hostage.
idiomatic: He went in person to Ye to fetch him, offering to stay behind as hostage.

literal: Shi Hu, in righteousness, assented.
idiomatic: Moved by his honor, Shi Hu agreed.

literal: When Zhaocheng took the throne he then divided half the state and gave it to him.
idiomatic: When Zhaocheng came to the throne he gave Gu half the realm.

literal: He died.
idiomatic: He died in his princely rank.

literal: His son Jin, having lost office, harbored anger, framed the Veritable Lord in rebellion, and died at Chang'an.
idiomatic: His son Jin, stripped of office and bitter, framed the Veritable Lord for treason and met his end at Chang'an.

literal: In Taizu's time, because Gu's merit was high, he was posthumously enfeoffed Prince of Gaoliang with posthumous title Shenwu.
idiomatic: In Taizu's day Gu's service was judged supreme; he was posthumously made Prince of Gaoliang, styled Shenwu.

literal: Jin's son Lezhen, [2] often had battle merit and later inherited his grandfather's enfeoffment.
idiomatic: Jin's son Lezhen, [2] won repeated honors in war and later inherited his grandfather's fief.

literal: At the beginning of Taizong, his title was changed to Prince of Pingyang.
idiomatic: At the opening of Taizong's reign he was made Prince of Pingyang.

literal: He died.
idiomatic: He passed away.

literal: His son Li inherited the original title Prince of Gaoliang.
idiomatic: His son Li took up the old title, Prince of Gaoliang.

literal: He died; posthumous title Prince Yi.
idiomatic: He died and was styled Prince Yi.

literal: His son Na inherited the title.
idiomatic: His son Na inherited the fief.

literal: He was appointed chief official of the central court.
idiomatic: He was made chief officer of the central court.

literal: Fierce and valiant, he was skilled in attack and battle.
idiomatic: Bold in assault, he excelled in battle.

literal: At the beginning of Zhengping, for an offense he was executed.
idiomatic: Early in Zhengping he was executed for a crime.

literal: When Xianzu took the throne he recalled Na's merit and ordered his son He to continue the enfeoffment.
idiomatic: At Xianzu's accession he honored Na's service and had his son He continue the line.

literal: He died.
idiomatic: He died in office.

literal: His son Dacao was by nature honest and straight.
idiomatic: His son Dacao was plain and upright by nature.

literal: In Gaozu's time, for princes who were not Taizu's descendants titles were as a rule reduced to duke.
idiomatic: Under Gaozu, princes outside Taizu's direct line were routinely demoted from prince to duke.

literal: Because Dacao's forebears' merit in yielding the state was heavy and great-grandfather Lezhen's merit was illustrious in the former court, he was changed to Duke of Taiyuan commandery.
idiomatic: Dacao's house had twice earned the throne's debt—Gu's abdication and Lezhen's battlefield fame—so he was made Duke of Taiyuan commandery instead.

literal: He died without a son; the state was extinguished.
idiomatic: He died childless and the fief lapsed.

literal: Emperor Shizong also had Dacao's elder cousin's son Hongwei continue the line.
idiomatic: Emperor Shizong later had Dacao's cousin's son Hongwei carry on the line.

literal: Respectful, modest, and loving learning, as Administrator of Yingchuan he had governing achievement.
idiomatic: Humble, eager to learn, he governed Yingchuan with a record of real achievement.

literal: At the beginning of Xiaojing, at Yingchuan he gathered followers responding to Guanxi; Prince of Qi Duke Xianwu sent generals to suppress and pacify him.
idiomatic: Early in Xiaojing he raised men at Yingchuan in answer to the Guanxi rising; the Prince of Qi, Duke Xianwu, sent generals who crushed him.

literal: Li's younger brother Ling—Shizu granted him Baron of Xiangyi.
idiomatic: Li's younger brother Ling received Baron of Xiangyi from Shizu.

literal: His title was advanced to viscount.
idiomatic: He was promoted to viscount.

literal: He died.
idiomatic: He passed away.

literal: His son Gui held office as major of Rouxuan garrison.
idiomatic: His son Gui served as major at Rouxuan garrison.

literal: Gui's son Zhi, styled Kongque.
idiomatic: Gui's son Zhi, whose style was Kongque, "Peacock."

literal: His appearance was tall and strong; his belt was ten arm-spans.
idiomatic: He was huge in frame, his belt ten arm-spans round.

literal: He was deputy of the Feathered Forest guard detachment.
idiomatic: He served as deputy commander of a Feathered Forest detachment.

literal: At the end of Gaozu's reign, for campaign merit he was granted Baron of Jinyang.
idiomatic: Late in Gaozu's reign his campaigns won him Baron of Jinyang.

literal: He was successively promoted to Director of the Guards and metropolitan-area commander.
idiomatic: He rose to Director of the Guards and commander of the capital district.

literal: In the first year of Wutai, Erzhu Rong reached Heyin and slaughtered court gentlemen; Zhi with Rong together climbed a high mound and looked down—from then on he joined with Rong.
idiomatic: In Wutai year one Erzhu Rong came to Heyin and butchered the court; Zhi climbed a mound beside him to watch the killing, and afterward threw in his lot with Rong.

literal: When Yuan Hao pressed close, Zhi followed the emperor north to welcome support.
idiomatic: When Yuan Hao closed in, Zhi rode north with the emperor to meet relief.

literal: Having reached Henei and wishing to enter the city, Zhi memorialized: "Henei by day closes its gates and by night would lead Your Majesty in—the meaning of this is hard to measure.
idiomatic: At Henei, when the emperor wished to enter the city, Zhi memorialized: "By day its gates stay shut and by night they would admit you—such intentions are impossible to read.

literal: Your original plan has its purpose; I beg you set out at once."
idiomatic: Your design still holds; I urge you to march on at once."

literal: The emperor assented; they advanced first to Changzi; because Erzhu Rong came to rescue, Zhi was made General of Agile Cavalry and enfeoffed Prince of Huashan.
idiomatic: The emperor agreed and pushed on to Changzi; when Erzhu Rong came to the rescue, Zhi was made General of Agile Cavalry and Prince of Huashan.

literal: After Emperor Zhuang had killed Erzhu Rong, Rong's clansman Zhao made disorder; the emperor wished to lead the armies in person to campaign; Zhi had secret communication with Zhao and urged the emperor, "The Yellow River is ten thousand ren deep—how could you cross it in haste?"
idiomatic: After Emperor Zhuang killed Erzhu Rong, Rong's kinsman Zhao rose in revolt; the emperor meant to take the field himself, but Zhi was in secret with Zhao and urged him, "The Yellow River is ten thousand ren deep—will you ford it in haste?"

literal: The emperor then composed himself in peace.
idiomatic: The emperor took ease and stayed put.

literal: When Zhao entered the hall, Zhi also arranged to restrain the guard troops.
idiomatic: When Zhao entered the hall Zhi also held back the palace guards.

literal: The emperor was pressed, the capital broke—all through Zhi's plotting.
idiomatic: The emperor was cornered and the capital fell—all by Zhi's design.

literal: At the beginning of Xiaojing he entered office as Grand Marshal with added attendant-in-ordinary.
idiomatic: Early in Xiaojing he entered court as Grand Marshal with the added rank of attendant-in-ordinary.

literal: Zhi had martial skill, was wooden in speech and few of words, and his nature was square and generous; each time he rested on duty at the palace gate, even in hot summer he did not remove cap and robes.
idiomatic: Zhi was a fighter, slow of tongue and sparing of words, but upright and steady; on gate duty in midsummer he would not loosen cap or gown.

literal: Once at Attendant-in-Chief Gao Yue's feast, Prince of Xianyang Tan relied on strength and drank wine, bullying the whole company; all lowered themselves and dared not answer.
idiomatic: At a feast of Attendant-in-Chief Gao Yue, Prince of Xianyang Tan, drunk on his strength, bullied the table until every man shrank silent.

literal: Tan said to Zhi, "Peacock, you old military officer—why did you get to be prince?"
idiomatic: Tan said to Zhi, "Peacock, you old soldier—how did you become a prince?"

literal: Zhi at once answered, "I cut off the rebel Yuan Xi's head—that is how I got it."
idiomatic: Zhi answered at once, "I took the rebel Yuan Xi's head—that is how."

literal: All turned pale; Zhi was at ease as before.
idiomatic: The room went white; Zhi sat easy as ever.

literal: In the third year of Xinghe he died; posthumously granted acting yellow battle-axe, Masters of Writing director, and Duke of the Masses.
idiomatic: He died in the third year of Xinghe and was posthumously given acting yellow battle-axe, director of the Masters of Writing, and Duke of the Masses.

literal: His son Daqi inherited the title.
idiomatic: His son Daqi inherited the fief.

literal: Later, with Yuan Jin he plotted to harm Prince Wenxiang of Qi and was killed.
idiomatic: Later he joined Yuan Jin in a plot against Prince Wenxiang of Qi and was put to death.

literal: Gu's grandson Du—in early Taizu was granted Marquis of Songzi and held office as director of comparative review in the ministry.
idiomatic: Gu's grandson Du, enfeoffed Marquis of Songzi under early Taizu, served as director of comparative review.

literal: He died.
idiomatic: He passed away.

literal: His son Yijin inherited Marquis of Xiangyang.
idiomatic: His son Yijin took up Marquis of Xiangyang.

literal: Xianzu honored old worthies, appointed him chief official of the outer court, and greatly favored him.
idiomatic: Xianzu, honoring his years, made him chief of the outer court and treated him with great weight.

literal: He died.
idiomatic: He died in office.

literal: His son Ping, styled Chuguo, inherited the hereditary Marquis of Songzi.
idiomatic: His son Ping, styled Chuguo, inherited the hereditary marquisate of Songzi.

literal: For military merit he was granted Baron of Ailing.
idiomatic: Battle honors won him Baron of Ailing.

literal: He died.
idiomatic: He passed away.

literal: His son Chang—in Gaozu's time inherited Marquis of Songzi; as a rule he was reduced from marquis and granted Baron of Ailing.
idiomatic: His son Chang inherited Songzi under Gaozu but, by the usual rule, was demoted from marquis to Baron of Ailing.

literal: Chang's nature was firm and unyielding; though there were auspicious and celebratory affairs he never opened his mouth to laugh.
idiomatic: Chang was iron by nature; even at weddings and feasts he never smiled.

literal: When Gaozu moved the capital, Chang as acting chief of Dai stayed behind to garrison.
idiomatic: When Gaozu moved the capital, Chang stayed behind as acting chief of Dai to hold the north.

literal: He was removed and made commander-in-chief of Huaishuo garrison; separately granted Chang wine—though he bowed and drank, his complexion was not peaceful.
idiomatic: He was transferred to commander at Huaishuo; Gaozu sent him wine apart from the court, and though he bowed and drank, his face never eased.

literal: Gaozu said, "I hear that you never laugh all your life—now we are separated by mountains, [3] you ought to laugh for me."
idiomatic: Gaozu said, "They tell me you have never laughed in all your days—now mountains lie between us, [3] so laugh once for me."

literal: Still he could not obtain it.
idiomatic: Even so Chang would not smile.

literal: Gaozu said, "Of the five phases' qi, some places partly do not enter."
idiomatic: Gaozu said, "Among the five phases, some temperaments never take a given element."

literal: Between the six directions, is there anything that does not exist?"
idiomatic: "Under heaven, what wonder does not exist?"

literal: Those attending nearby all clutched their wrists and laughed greatly.
idiomatic: The attendants clutched their sides and roared with laughter.

literal: In Shizong's time he was northern central army general with concurrent Administrator of Henei.
idiomatic: Under Shizong he was northern central army general and concurrent Administrator of Henei.

literal: Chang thought the He Bridge mooring road was narrow and inconvenient for travelers; also autumn waters flooded yearly and often destroyed it, so he made a boat route and broadly recruited empty carts leaving the capital, [4] ordering each in turn to haul one pair of stones, piling them to form banks.
idiomatic: Chang found the He Bridge towpath too narrow for traffic and the autumn floods too ruinous, so he opened a boat channel and pressed every empty cart leaving the capital [4] to haul a load of stone until banks rose on either side.

literal: The bridge widened and coming and going were convenient; commanderies near the bridge had no more forced labor and disturbance; public and private relied on it.
idiomatic: The crossing widened, travel eased, and neighboring commanderies were spared the old corvée; public and private alike prospered by it.

literal: He held office as director of revenue, attendant-in-ordinary, and Inspector of Yong province.
idiomatic: He served as director of revenue, attendant-in-ordinary, and Inspector of Yong.

literal: He died; posthumous title Cheng.
idiomatic: He died and was styled Cheng.

literal: After mid-life Chang's office and rank were slightly attained and then he became arrogant and self-important; within the gates there was no propriety, brothers were not harmonious, and his nature was also greedy and cruel; commentators despised him.
idiomatic: Only in middle age did Chang's modest offices ripen into pride: at home he abandoned ritual, quarreled with his kin, and grew greedy and harsh, and men of judgment scorned him.

literal: Chang's son Zihua, styled Furong, inherited the title.
idiomatic: Chang's son Zihua, styled Furong, took up the fief.

literal: At the beginning of Emperor Zhuang he was appointed Inspector of Qi province.
idiomatic: At the opening of Emperor Zhuang's reign he became Inspector of Qi.

literal: Before this, the province's territory had repeatedly seen rebellion; in Xing Tuo's disorder people could not protect themselves.
idiomatic: The province had long been torn by revolt; in Xing Tuo's rising no one could keep himself safe.

literal: Yet Zihua gathered and settled powerful families, entrusted them with authority—the multitude all were moved and pleased; within the borders were calm.
idiomatic: Zihua rallied the great clans, gave them authority, and won their hearts until the land lay quiet.

literal: Yet his nature was very narrow and urgent; when urgent he did not choose words in his mouth and with his own hand would strike and beat.
idiomatic: Yet he was quick-tempered: in a rage he spoke without restraint and struck out with his own fists.

literal: Chief clerk Zheng Zihan was Zihua's close friend yet was insulted and reviled and at once left him.
idiomatic: His chief clerk and friend Zheng Zihan bore his abuse once too often and walked away.

literal: Zihua, though he repented and exerted himself, still could not change.
idiomatic: Zihua repented and strained to reform, but the habit held.

literal: In office he did not perform hypocritical acts; whenever there were gifts, he mostly declined much and accepted little, so men did not resent his taking.
idiomatic: He never played the hypocrite in office: when gifts came he refused the bulk and took little, so men did not begrudge him.

literal: In judging cases and examining prisoners he strove to add benevolence and forbearance.
idiomatic: In trials he leaned toward mercy.

literal: The people of Qi set up a stele praising his virtue.
idiomatic: The people of Qi raised a stele to his virtue.

literal: Later he was removed and made Inspector of Ji province.
idiomatic: Later he was transferred to Inspector of Ji.

literal: When Erzhu Zhao entered Luoyang, the people of Qi province Zhao Luozhou drove out Inspector Prince of Danyang Xiao Zan and memorialized Administrator of Jinan Fang Shida to act as provincial affairs.
idiomatic: When Erzhu Zhao took Luoyang, Zhao Luozhou of Qi drove out Inspector Xiao Zan, Prince of Danyang, and asked Jinan Administrator Fang Shida to govern the province.

literal: Luozhou's son Yuanxian had first followed Zihua at Ji province; he intercepted the road and changed the memorial, asking that Zihua again be Inspector of Qi.
idiomatic: Luozhou's son Yuanxian, who had served under Zihua in Ji, waylaid the dispatch and rewrote it to restore Zihua to Qi.

literal: Zihua's mother the Fang clan had once gone to a relative's for food and drink; returning at night she vomited greatly; people thought she had been poisoned and were very worried, but Zihua then scooped up the vomit, ate it all, and his mother was then at ease.
idiomatic: Zihua's mother, Lady Fang, fell violently ill after a relative's feast; fearing poison, the household panicked until Zihua ate her vomit and she recovered her ease.

literal: Soon, because of mourning for his mother, he returned to the capital.
idiomatic: Soon he left for the capital in mourning for her.

literal: At the beginning of Xiaojing he was appointed Inspector of southern Xuzhou.
idiomatic: Early in Xiaojing he was made Inspector of southern Xuzhou.

literal: His younger brother's son Zisi was sent as envoy to Guanxi; the court sent Right Guard General Guo Qiong to seize him.
idiomatic: His nephew Zisi was sent to Guanxi; the court dispatched Right Guard General Guo Qiong to arrest him.

literal: Zisi said to Qiong's servant, "Quickly kill me—why long hold a man of the state!"
idiomatic: Zisi told Qiong's man, "Kill me now—why keep a servant of the realm in bonds?"

literal: Zihua said to Zisi, "Because of your coarse carelessness you have made me thus."
idiomatic: Zihua cried to Zisi, "Your rashness has brought me to this."

literal: He knocked his head on the bed, weeping beyond control.
idiomatic: He beat his head on the bed and wept without restraint.

literal: Zisi stroked his beard with his hand, turned and said to Zihua, "Sir, your breath is ill."
idiomatic: Zisi smoothed his beard and told Zihua, "You have a sour stomach."

literal: Soon both Zisi and he died at the outer office below the gate.
idiomatic: Soon both men were killed in the outer office below the gate.

literal: Zisi, styled Zhongnian, was by nature fierce and violent and always took loyalty and ardor as his boast.
idiomatic: Zisi, styled Zhongnian, was fierce by nature and prided himself on fierce loyalty.

literal: When Yuan Tianmu held court power, through kin and follower he was recommended as chief rectifier of the Censorate.
idiomatic: While Yuan Tianmu held power he entered the Censorate as chief rectifier through family ties.
